name: Indigo tea
lede: Indigo tea is a dark, warm brown from Japan's traditional color list, and one of the single most common named colors in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: In Japan: Aikobicha
sections.body:
The name is written 藍媚茶, romanized Aikobicha, and our color library glosses it as "indigo tea" [1]. The closing kanji, 茶 (*cha*), marks it as a member of Japan's tea/brown family of names, the same character that ends [[baiko-brown]], another traditional color in this family [1]. Who paired indigo with tea in this particular shade, and when, is undocumented in the sources we have [1].

The nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[jacaranda-brown]], yellower than this shade; [[olive-drab-7]] and [[dark-olive-brown]] sit close by, both darker [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a match for Indigo tea in 5,716 of 23,781 paintings, about 24 percent, more common than every other named color we track, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1600s, in 1,390 of 6,394 paintings from that century, 1.4 times the rate its share of the archive would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 35 percent of its appearances [3].

The painter most devoted to it is Meindert Hobbema, in 11 of his 16 paintings here, 3.4 times his peers' rate, as photographed [3]. The earliest archive match is dated 900; the archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first [3]. It shares canvases more than chance with Deep Olive and [[baiko-brown]] [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications [3].
